The salt has a way of making a man honest. I lay the ledger flat against my knee and look at the page instead of Mei.

"No," I say. "I did not tell them."

My thumb presses the last entry into the paper. A small sound, but I make it anyway. "I told the harbour watch what the salt cost, and where it went. If they are asking me about the bags now, that is their business."

I close the ledger with one hand and wait for the room to finish deciding what it means.

The salt is a small thing until it is not. I keep my eyes on the ledger, though the figures have gone soft. Mei's question waits just beyond the ink, and I let it wait.

"I told them there was salt," I say. My pen touches the page, a thin line where a number should be. "I did not tell them how much. A man can be honest and still leave room."

I close the ledger. The room is quieter now. "If the harbour watch has more than that, then someone else has been talking."

The bench creaks under me the way old oaks do when they’ve decided to hold a secret one more season. Flour dust drifts past the bakehouse window like slow snow, and I pretend it means something.

"You're taking up more than half of it," I say, because it’s easier than saying you’ve taken up all of my usual quiet corners. I nudge a pebble with my heel, keep it rolling toward the hedge where my teacher’s thyme is trying to be brave again. "Don't worry. I'll be on the good side of the story."

"You can sit too, Kira," I add. "If you are not finished with the strap."

The sound leaves the room before the breath does. I stand over him with my fingers still on his throat, and for one second I am grateful I am not the one who has to hear it. Then I am the one who has to hear it.

I do not close his eyes. I do not touch his face. I set my hands on the table's edge, one on each side of his body, as if I can keep him from tipping over into whatever comes next.

"There is no next," I say.

My voice is too level. It is the voice I use when I am counting out doses, when I am telling a mother that the fever is only a fever. I have not used it on a corpse before. I am not sure it was made for one.

I look at the cup of water. The surface is still. I look at the boy's hand, open on the linen. I have washed that hand three times. I have dried it, oiled it, wrapped it. I do not know what else to do with a hand that has nothing left to hold.

I pull the linen up over his wrists, not because it will help, but because I need to do something with my hands that is not praying. The room is too quiet. I can hear the candle guttering. I can hear my own pulse in my ears.

"There is no next," I say again.

This time it is not for him. It is for me.

The salt has a way of finding its own witnesses," I say before my mind can settle the matter into a lie or a truth with edges on it. I keep my eyes on the wet planking at the end of the quay, where the tide has left a black line like a ledger no one wants balanced. "I did not stand before them and say it was me."

"That is not what you asked."

A gull drops onto the crane arm and tilts its head as if it too is waiting to see whether I will commit to anything larger than silence. I take the cap from behind my ear and turn it over once, twice, the brim catching grey light while she waits for me to finish, or perhaps for me to start again in a truer key.

"The harbour watch knows because they always know," I say at last. "Whether I told them directly is smaller than you think."

The door is in my back. I can feel it through the wool, a cold bar across the shoulder blades, so I stop thinking of it as a door and start thinking of it as a wall. Kira’s hand is on the strap. I can see it from here. I do not sit.

“Sitting makes me look like I mean to stay,” I say. My voice comes out flatter than I want. I shift my weight to the left boot, away from the wall. “I am only deciding which direction the staying would go.”

I do not ask permission to stand. I have stopped needing it.

"I am sorry," I say before the word sounds too small or too large. "I did not waste anything until now."

The silence has a shape now, and I do not reach for it. His chest is finished with me, which is worse than if it had been lying.

I set the lancet down where I can see it, because a healer who cannot admit she has used up her knives is only a woman making noise over a body.

"You heard it," I say to the room, not to any one of them. "I am going to say it once so we do not have to invent a kinder way later. He has stopped breathing, and I have run out of reasons why that should not be final."

I keep my fingers where they are, as if moving them would make it less true.

“Then stop counting what they told you,” I say to the empty chair across from me because chairs are cheaper than clients and less likely to phone after dark “and start counting what disappeared from the page while you blinked.”

I open it once. Only once. The names are still wet, not with ink, with the day. The candle does not help. It only makes the paper look more expensive than it is.

"You can stay," I say to the room. "I am only deciding which of you is staying."
